results.summary: This analog block generates a temperature-stable reference voltage of about 1.2 V using a pseudo-PTAT current generator with enable-gated startup. It is used by applying a 1.8 V supply and asserting the appropriate enable pins (ui[6] and ui[3]) to obtain the reference on ua[0]. Testing requires a voltmeter to measure the output and verify low temperature dependence. The design is notable for including a startup circuit that can be toggled if the bandgap fails to start.

This design implements a two-player Pong game with score display, outputting a standard 640x480 VGA signal at 60 Hz. It is controlled by four buttons for paddle movement and requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for display. The game logic uses a finite state machine and procedural graphics generation without any microprocessor or external memory. The design is notable for its compact implementation and themed graphics inspired by The Legend of Zelda.

This chip implements a Simon Says memory game where a sequence is stored in RAM and the player must repeat it using two input buttons. It operates in two modes: programming mode to load the sequence via bidirectional pins, and game mode where the sequence is shown on LEDs and player input is checked. The design is tested with a Cocotb testbench that verifies programming, correct input, and error detection. External hardware such as switches and LEDs is suggested for manual testing.

This analog circuit implements a compact spiking neuron that generates firing patterns based on five external bias and input controls. It is tested by tuning the analog inputs (IREFA, IREFB, BIASC, BIASD, and VCORE) and observing the output waveform on VOUT with an oscilloscope or DAQ. External hardware includes adjustable analog sources and a clean analog supply with decoupling. The design is notable for its small size and potential use in neuromorphic systems.

This design generates a VGA signal displaying the moving text 'Bonjour Terre!' on a monitor. It is created using the VGA playground with a logo template and requires only a VGA monitor for testing. The design is simple and serves as a demonstration of text animation on a VGA display. No external hardware beyond a monitor is needed.

This SystemVerilog design implements an AXI4-Lite slave with a read-only ID register and 32 general-purpose registers, providing a 16-bit readback path on the bidirectional pins. It is used by driving the address, write/read requests, and data through the input and bidirectional pins, with read data appearing on the outputs. No external hardware is required for basic operation, though a host controller is needed to exercise the AXI4-Lite interface. The design serves as a demonstration of integrating a standard bus protocol into a Tiny Tapeout project.

This 8-bit serial-in ALU processes two operands shifted in LSB-first and supports eight operations including ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, and NOT. It provides a parallel result and status flags (carry, zero, negative, overflow, done) after 16 clock cycles. Testing involves shifting in operands and reading the result and flags, and it can be interfaced with a microcontroller or manual switches. The design is notable for its serial interface, which reduces pin count while maintaining full ALU functionality.

This analog circuit provides a zero-temperature-coefficient (ZTAT) voltage reference, designed to be stable across temperature variations. It is tested by measuring the VREF pin at different temperatures, with the rate of change expected to be within 1.2 mV. External hardware includes a high-precision multimeter and an environmental chamber or thermal stream. The design is a simple bandgap reference, notable for its low temperature drift.

This design is a 4-bit processor inspired by reversible computing, featuring a 4-phase bus protocol and a 4x4 scratchpad RAM. It executes arithmetic, logic, shift, compare, and memory operations, with support for reversible operations like save and reverse using checkpoint metadata. Testing is done via cocotb, verifying phase progression, ALU operations, RAM access, and reverse functionality. No external hardware is required, but a host controller can drive the phase-aware transactions.

This project is a silicon artwork featuring Hatsune Miku and Juno Teo Minh, implemented in Verilog. The documentation is essentially a template with no functional description, testing instructions, or external hardware details. It appears to be a decorative design rather than a functional circuit. As a result, its purpose and operation cannot be determined from the provided information.
